Deir Yassin

Massacre · 1948-04-09 · Under British Mandate

April 9, 1948
Date
Deir Yassin, west of Jerusalem
Historical Location
≈107–250
Deaths
≈710
Displaced
Location, thenDeir Yassin (Dayr Yasin), Jerusalem, British Mandate of Palestine
Location, nowGivat Shaul neighborhood, West Jerusalem, Israel, Village demolished; site integrated into Israeli neighborhoods
PerpetratorsIrgun (Etzel); Lehi (Stern Gang); Haganah/Palmach (support)
ClassificationWar Crime (1907 Hague); Crimes Against Humanity (modern)

Summary

The Deir Yassin massacre occurred during intense fighting around Jerusalem in early April 1948 (Operation Nachshon context). The village had previously concluded a local non-aggression understanding with nearby Jewish communities; nonetheless, Irgun and Lehi launched a multi-axis assault at dawn. Haganah/Palmach elements later provided support.

Killings of civilians—including women, children and elderly—were documented by Israeli and international witnesses; surviving captives were paraded in Jerusalem and later released. Death estimates vary; most research centers near ≈107, with higher claims (≈200–250) appearing in contemporary accounts.

The entire village population (≈710 in 1948) was displaced; Deir Yassin's lands were later absorbed into West Jerusalem neighborhoods. No perpetrators were prosecuted; Irgun commander Menachem Begin later became Prime Minister (1977–1983).

Timeline

Pre-April 1948 Non-aggression agreementVillage elders and nearby Jewish communities agree to avoid hostilities. — IPS/PalQuest
April 9, 1948 (dawn) Attack beginsIrgun/Lehi assault from multiple axes; fierce resistance; later Haganah/Palmach mortar support. — IPS/PalQuest
Morning–Afternoon Killings & lootingHouse-to-house killings; reports of executions and desecrations; systematic looting. — IPS/PalQuest; ICRC
Aftermath (Apr 9–11) Captives paradedSurvivors driven in trucks, paraded in Jerusalem, then released; international outcry. — IPS/PalQuest; de Reynier account

Testimony

Jacques de ReynierDescribed heavily armed young militiamen; piles of corpses; rescuing a few survivors; noted a victory parade of captives. — 'A Jerusalem Un Drapeau Flottait Sur La Ligne De Feu' (1950)
Meir Pa'ilReported indiscriminate killings and parade of captives in Jerusalem; noted subsequent executions. 'It was direct murder. Haganah command tried to hush up the case.' — Interview with Yediot Aharonot, April 4, 1972
Fahimi ZidanThe Jews ordered all of us to line up against the wall. They started shooting at us. I was wounded in the side, but most of us children were saved because we hid behind our parents. The bullets hit my sister Kadri in the head, my sister Sameh in the cheek, my brother Muhammad in the chest. — British Palestine Police Report, April 13, 1948 - UK National Archives CO 537/3869
Richard CatlingThere is no doubt that many sexual atrocities were committed by the attacking Jews. Many young school girls were raped and later slaughtered. Old women were also molested. — Secret report to British High Commissioner, April 13, 1948 - UK National Archives CO 537/3869

War crimes

Mass Killings of CiviliansCivilians killed in house-to-house operations; bodies found throughout village. Women, children, elderly among victims. — ICRC Documentation
Summary ExecutionsMultiple witnesses reported captives lined up and executed. Meir Pa'il (Palmach): 'It was direct murder.' — IPS/PalQuest
Sexual Violence & DesecrationBritish Assistant Inspector Richard Catling (Report CO 537/3869): 'Many sexual atrocities were committed... Many young school girls were raped and later slaughtered.' Bodies mutilated. — UK National Archives
Looting & DestructionSystematic looting of homes; theft of valuables and livestock. Village later demolished; lands absorbed.
Forced Displacement & HumiliationSurvivors paraded through Jewish neighborhoods before release. Public humiliation photographed and publicized. — Institute for Palestine Studies

Legal classification

Law Applicable in April 1948Hague Convention IV (1907): Customary by 1948. Art. 23(c): killing enemies who laid down arms; Art. 25: attack on undefended places; Art. 28: pillage; Art. 46: protection of family honor, lives, property.
Post-1949 Context (Descriptive)Geneva Convention IV (1949): Adopted Aug 12, 1949 (16 months after Deir Yassin). Israel ratified Jul 6, 1951; Jordan May 29, 1951. Not applicable retroactively to April 1948 events.
Treaty OpposabilityVienna Convention principle: Treaties not retroactive (Art. 28). Geneva IV cannot be invoked for events predating its adoption.
Law Applicable in April 1948Martens Clause (1899/1907): Humanitarian principles binding even where not explicitly codified.
Post-1949 Context (Descriptive)Rome Statute (1998): Modern framework characterizing acts as crimes against humanity and war crimes. Used descriptively; not retroactive enforcement.
Treaty OpposabilityCustomary IHL: Hague 1907 + Martens Clause bound all parties in 1948 regardless of ratification.
Law Applicable in April 1948Note: These instruments were opposable to all parties in 1948 as customary international humanitarian law.
Post-1949 Context (Descriptive)Note: Modern classifications aid understanding but do not create retroactive legal obligations.

Historical impact

Immediate ImpactSymbolic turning point in 1948 war; widely publicized, fueling panic and flight in surrounding areas
Long-term SignificanceCentral symbol in Palestinian collective memory of the Nakba; commemorated annually April 9
Accountability✘ No perpetrators prosecuted under any legal framework
Immediate Impact≈250,000 Palestinians fled homes in following weeks (1/3 of total Nakba refugees)
Long-term SignificanceSubject of ongoing historiographical debate (New Historians vs. traditional narratives)
Accountability✘ Menachem Begin (Irgun commander) became Israeli PM (1977–1983); Nobel Peace Prize (1978)
Immediate Impact70,000 Palestinians fled Haifa citing Deir Yassin as reason
Long-term SignificanceRelevant to contemporary discussions of Palestinian right of return
Accountability✘ Yitzhak Shamir (Lehi leader) became Israeli PM (1983–1984, 1986–1992)
Immediate ImpactComplete depopulation of Deir Yassin; lands integrated into West Jerusalem
Accountability✘ Village site never returned; Kfar Shaul psychiatric hospital built 1951 on village lands
